STREAMS.label: Science
STREAMS.blurb: Maths, physics, chemistry or biology at the 12th level.
STREAMS.what: Science opens the widest set of technical doors in India, because most engineering, data and medicine entrance exams sit inside it.
STREAMS.how: Keep one subject deep rather than all of them shallow. Pick the one you would still read about at 1am and build the rest around it.

STREAMS.label: Commerce
STREAMS.what: Commerce leads to finance, accounting, banking, taxation and business analysis roles, all of which hire heavily in Indian metros.
STREAMS.how: Get genuinely good at one spreadsheet or accounting tool before you start applying. Most commerce jobs are decided in the first two rounds by how you read a number.

STREAMS.label: Arts / Humanities
STREAMS.blurb: History, literature, economics, psychology or fine arts.
STREAMS.what: Arts gives you writing, research, law, teaching, design and communication skills that most other streams never practise.
STREAMS.how: Treat writing as a technical skill, not a personality trait. Write a lot on a schedule and get it in front of people who will criticise it.

STREAMS.label: Vocational / ITI
STREAMS.blurb: A trade qualification, ITI, or a hands-on polytechnic line.
STREAMS.what: Skilled trades, operations, technicians and field engineering are in real shortage, and many of these roles pay better than a default graduate degree.
STREAMS.how: Pair the trade with one digital skill. Electricity plus an IoT toolkit, or a mechanical diploma plus CAD, is worth more than either alone.

STREAMS.label: Technology / Polytechnic
STREAMS.blurb: Polytechnic, diploma in engineering, or already into ITI-level tech.
STREAMS.what: You are closest to the work already. A diploma holder who can code or handle networks skips the two years most people spend repeating a syllabus.
STREAMS.how: Turn the syllabus into portfolio work. Same concepts, but as something you built and can demo rather than a mark you received.

STREAMS.label: Something else
STREAMS.blurb: A mix, a gap year, or a stream that does not fit the usual boxes.
STREAMS.what: There is no stream that locks the door. Hiring in India is far more interested in what you can show than which box you ticked at 16.
STREAMS.how: Skip the self-analysis and start building one small finished thing this month. Finished work is the only thing that settles this question.

DURATIONS.label: 1 year
DURATIONS.note: Under a year, fast and focused.
DURATIONS.what: A single year is only enough if you already know roughly what you are aiming at, and you spend nearly all of it building rather than watching.
DURATIONS.how: Pick one role, one stack, and go deep on it. Breadth costs you the year, depth is what makes it worth something.

DURATIONS.label: 2 years
DURATIONS.note: The classic MCA / MBA / MTech window.
DURATIONS.what: Two years fits one serious specialisation with a project at the end, which is exactly the shape most hiring managers expect.
DURATIONS.how: Front-load fundamentals, then spend the second half on one substantial project you can defend in an interview.

DURATIONS.label: 3 years
DURATIONS.what: Three years gives you time to switch direction once without losing much, which matters more than landing on the perfect choice immediately.
DURATIONS.how: Use the first year to explore broadly, then commit by the end of year two so the final year produces real work.

DURATIONS.label: 4 years
DURATIONS.note: B.Tech / B.Des and most professional degrees.
DURATIONS.what: Four years is the norm in India for technical roles, and it is the only one of these windows where a college placement system meaningfully works for you.
DURATIONS.how: Keep the first two years for fundamentals, use the third for internships, and make the fourth year a job hunt with a portfolio behind it.

DURATIONS.label: 5+ years
DURATIONS.note: Integrated degrees and the long game.
DURATIONS.what: Five years is worth it when the destination genuinely needs it, such as MBBS, integrated law, or a masters stacked on a B.Tech.
DURATIONS.how: Only take the extra years if you can name the specific job at the end. Vague long horizons lose money and motivation both.

DEGREES.label: B.Tech / B.E
DEGREES.what: The broadest engineering entry point in India, and the one with the most hiring partners attached to campus placement.
DEGREES.how: Specialise only in the final year. Until then, fundamentals plus one language done properly beats six languages done badly.

DEGREES.label: B.Sc
DEGREES.what: A science degree that pairs well with data, teaching, research and the many regulated science roles that need one on paper.
DEGREES.how: Add computing early. A B.Sc plus real programming lands you in far more places than the degree alone.

DEGREES.label: B.A
DEGREES.what: A liberal arts degree that builds the writing, research and argument skills most people never develop on their own.
DEGREES.how: Pair it with a specialisation, such as economics, psychology or English, so the degree says something specific on paper.

DEGREES.label: B.Com
DEGREES.what: The direct route into accounting, taxation, banking and financial operations, most of which hire in bulk every year.
DEGREES.how: Get certified in one real tool, Excel at an advanced level or a Tally or SAP track, and apply early rather than after a gap year.

DEGREES.label: B.C.A
DEGREES.what: The fastest conventional route into software work in India, and heavily recruited by campus hiring programmes.
DEGREES.how: DSA is the whole game for placements. Start in the second year and treat interview prep as part of the degree, not a separate phase.

DEGREES.label: M.C.A
DEGREES.what: The standard upgrade from any non-B.Tech degree into software roles, and a strong recruiter signal in India.
DEGREES.how: Use the two years for a specialisation plus a real internship. An MCA with no internship is a weaker card than a B.Tech with one.

DEGREES.label: M.Sc
DEGREES.what: Deep specialisation in one science, which is the route into research, academia and the R&D roles that a general degree will not reach.
DEGREES.how: Pair the specialisation with computation. Research-adjacent work in India increasingly expects you to model, not just measure.

DEGREES.label: M.B.A
DEGREES.what: The strongest reset button in India for switching tracks late, and the shortest path into management and product roles.
DEGREES.how: Go in with a goal and a project, not just to collect the letters. Recruitment here runs almost entirely on what you did during the two years.

DEGREES.label: B.Des
DEGREES.what: A professional design degree that covers product, UI, graphic and interaction design as a job, not as a hobby.
DEGREES.how: Build a portfolio of four deep projects rather than twenty thin ones. Admissions and hiring both read the depth first.

DEGREES.label: LLB
DEGREES.what: The route to legal practice in India, and also one of the most general-useful degrees for negotiation, compliance and contract work.
DEGREES.how: Clinic work and internships matter more than marks here. Take every moot you can and write properly.

DEGREES.label: B.Ed
DEGREES.what: The teaching qualification, and one of the few degrees with genuinely guaranteed demand in smaller cities and villages.
DEGREES.how: Add one digital skill, such as curriculum design or edtech tooling, and you become the teacher everyone insists on hiring.

DEGREES.label: Diploma
DEGREES.what: A focused, cheaper and often faster route to a specific trade, with strong lateral entry into industry in India.
DEGREES.how: Do not stop at the diploma. Add one digital capability to it and you become a technician who can be sent anywhere.

DEGREES.label: B.Voc
DEGREES.what: A skilling-first degree that is industry-linked and built around practical assessment rather than long theory papers.
DEGREES.how: Use the on-the-job training slot properly. That industry contact is the entire point of the degree.

DEGREES.label: Not decided yet
DEGREES.what: Not having a degree picked yet is completely normal at this stage, and plenty of strong careers do not need one.
DEGREES.how: Spend two weeks on each of the two or three options that keep coming to mind, then commit. Deciding slowly is fine, not deciding is not.

INTERESTS.label: Coding & building
INTERESTS.what: Turning an idea into something a person can actually click. This is the shortest distance from no experience to a hireable portfolio.
INTERESTS.how: Learn one language properly, then build four small full projects that solve a real problem for someone you know. Finished beats perfect every time.

INTERESTS.label: Data & numbers
INTERESTS.what: Turning messy records into a decision someone can act on. The most transferable skill in the job market right now.
INTERESTS.how: SQL first, because it is the one that is genuinely required everywhere. Then one BI tool and a spreadsheet discipline.

INTERESTS.label: Design & visuals
INTERESTS.what: Deciding how something looks and feels so that people can use it without being taught.
INTERESTS.how: Redesign three apps that already exist and write the reasoning out. Design judgement is shown, not claimed.

INTERESTS.label: AI & machine learning
INTERESTS.what: Building systems that learn from data rather than following rules someone wrote by hand.
INTERESTS.how: Get the maths and Python genuinely solid before touching a framework. Most AI tutorials skip the part that makes it work.

INTERESTS.label: Cyber security
INTERESTS.what: Finding the holes in systems before someone else does, and getting paid to be the reason that does not happen.
INTERESTS.how: Do the free labs first, then get hands on deliberately vulnerable machines. This field punishes theory-only study hardest of all.

INTERESTS.label: Marketing & growth
INTERESTS.what: Understanding what people want, what makes them act, and what makes them keep doing it.
INTERESTS.how: Run one real campaign for a small business or your own project, even on a tiny budget, and measure it properly.

INTERESTS.label: Apps & mobile
INTERESTS.what: Building the software people carry in their pocket all day, which is where a huge share of daily use actually happens.
INTERESTS.how: Ship one app to a store. The deployment step teaches more than months of tutorials, and it is the step most people avoid.

INTERESTS.label: Cloud & infrastructure
INTERESTS.what: Keeping systems running, scaled and reliable, including the parts nobody is supposed to notice.
INTERESTS.how: Break your own environment on purpose, then fix it and write down what happened. That loop is the whole job.

INTERESTS.label: Product & strategy
INTERESTS.what: Deciding what gets built, in what order, and why. The role that sits between users, design and engineering.
INTERESTS.how: Analyse one product you use every day and argue for a change with evidence. This is a thinking job, not a tools job.

INTERESTS.label: Money & markets
INTERESTS.what: Reading numbers to make decisions about money, whether that is a company budget or a market.
INTERESTS.how: Learn statistics properly and use it on real data you care about. The maths is the differentiator, not the terminology.

HOBBIES.label: Gaming
HOBBIES.what: Design, logic, systems thinking and teamwork under pressure. Game jams turn a hobby into a portfolio instantly.
HOBBIES.how: Enter one jam with people you do not know. The deadline and the constraints do more for you than any amount of solo practice.

HOBBIES.label: Sports
HOBBIES.what: Discipline, teamwork, and a body of people who will vouch for you in ways a resume cannot.
HOBBIES.how: Compete in something with rankings. People who have trained under pressure are noticeably harder to fake in an interview.

HOBBIES.label: Music
HOBBIES.what: Deep pattern recognition, sustained practice, and the ability to work on something for years without an audience.
HOBBIES.how: Record and release something. Finishing is a rare skill and it transfers straight into shipping software.

HOBBIES.label: Drawing & art
HOBBIES.what: Visual thinking and the ability to notice proportion, layout and detail, which is a real professional skill.
HOBBIES.how: Draw a page every day for a month. It builds the eye faster than any tutorial on design history.

HOBBIES.label: Writing
HOBBIES.what: The ability to think clearly and persuade on paper, which is the rarest technical skill there is.
HOBBIES.how: Publish every week for three months. One piece becomes documentation, a blog, or interview evidence.

HOBBIES.label: Photography
HOBBIES.what: Composition, patience, and a trained eye for light that transfers straight into visual and product work.
HOBBIES.how: Shoot one project with a brief and a deadline, then present it as a series rather than a folder of snapshots.

HOBBIES.label: Video editing
HOBBIES.what: Storytelling, precision, and a genuinely rare ability that most graduates simply do not have.
HOBBIES.how: Make three finished videos on real deadlines. Edit for someone else for a month and the learning accelerates sharply.

HOBBIES.label: Reading
HOBBIES.what: Context, vocabulary, and the habit of forming a view before you argue it. It shows in how you write.
HOBBIES.how: Keep a note on one idea per chapter and publish the notes. Reading becomes visible output.

HOBBIES.label: Travel
HOBBIES.what: Adaptability, cultural reading, and the habit of navigating systems that are not documented.
HOBBIES.how: Go somewhere with almost no planning and no English support. It is a genuine and unusually good skill test.

HOBBIES.label: Cooking
HOBBIES.what: Process discipline, timing, quality control, and a genuine sense of what good output feels like.
HOBBIES.how: Cook one unfamiliar cuisine from scratch each month and write down the method as you go.

HOBBIES.label: Volunteering
HOBBIES.what: Real-world experience with people, and evidence of character that a technical interview actively looks for.
HOBBIES.how: Commit to one organisation for a full season. Continuity is worth more on a form than five one-off days.

HOBBIES.label: Making & hardware
HOBBIES.what: Physical problem solving, and the rare ability to think outside the screen when something breaks.
HOBBIES.how: Build one thing that exists in the world. Breadboards, sensors and 3D printing all teach the same lesson.

SKILLS.label: HTML
SKILLS.what: The structure every web page is built from, and the first thing to learn if anything will be viewed in a browser.
SKILLS.how: Build three real pages by hand before using a framework. You should be able to explain every tag you used.

SKILLS.label: CSS
SKILLS.what: Everything about how a page looks, lays out and responds to screen size.
SKILLS.how: Recreate two existing sites pixel-close, then break them on purpose to see what holds.

SKILLS.label: JavaScript
SKILLS.what: The programming language that runs in every browser and most servers. The one language that is genuinely everywhere.
SKILLS.how: Do the exercises, then build something with no tutorial running beside you. The gap between those two is the whole learning curve.

SKILLS.label: TypeScript
SKILLS.what: JavaScript with types, which catches whole categories of bugs before the code ever runs.
SKILLS.how: Add it to a project you have already finished rather than starting from it.

SKILLS.label: React
SKILLS.what: The dominant way to build interactive interfaces in JavaScript today.
SKILLS.how: Build one interface with three components, then refactor until the state actually feels like it belongs somewhere obvious.

SKILLS.label: Node.js
SKILLS.what: Running JavaScript on the server, which is what turns a front end into a full application.
SKILLS.how: Build one API and put it in front of a real front end before touching a database.

SKILLS.label: Python
SKILLS.what: The most broadly useful language for data, automation, backend work and scripting.
SKILLS.how: Automate one small annoyance in your own week. Automation is the concept that makes Python stick.

SKILLS.label: Java
SKILLS.what: Still the backbone of large Indian enterprise and banking systems, and the standard for core backend campus hiring.
SKILLS.how: Get collections, streams and concurrency genuinely right. Interviews here are unusually deep on exactly those.

SKILLS.label: C / C++
SKILLS.what: Low-level performance, and what competitive programming and much of core infrastructure are built on.
SKILLS.how: Solve problems, not toy programs. This language only makes sense once you are reasoning about memory and time.

SKILLS.label: SQL
SKILLS.what: Asking databases questions, which is required in almost every technical and most business role.
SKILLS.how: Query a real public dataset until joins stop being scary. Reading data is a hireable skill on its own.

SKILLS.label: NoSQL & data modelling
SKILLS.what: Storing data that does not fit neatly in rows, which is most data users do not see or think about.
SKILLS.how: Model a real domain, like a bookstore or a hospital system, and defend the relationships you chose.

SKILLS.label: Git & GitHub
SKILLS.what: Tracking and collaborating on code, and effectively the shared language of every technical team.
SKILLS.how: Use branches, commits and pull requests from day one, even on solo projects. It is much harder to retrofit.

SKILLS.label: REST APIs
SKILLS.what: How one piece of software asks another for data, which is the basic contract of all modern software.
SKILLS.how: Build a small service, document it in Postman, and have something other than your own code consume it.

SKILLS.label: Linux & command line
SKILLS.what: The environment most servers actually run, and where every developer eventually becomes their own support desk.
SKILLS.how: Run a bare Ubuntu box and administer it for a month. Do not stay in the graphical desktop.

SKILLS.label: Docker
SKILLS.what: Shipping software in a fixed environment so it works on every machine, which removes an entire class of problems.
SKILLS.how: Containerise something you built, then deliberately break it in one place to see the value.

SKILLS.label: Kubernetes
SKILLS.what: Running and repairing many containers at once, once manual management stops scaling.
SKILLS.how: Do not start here. Get Docker and Linux solid first, or this will be vocabulary with no meaning attached.

SKILLS.label: AWS
SKILLS.what: The largest cloud platform and the one most Indian job listings mention by name.
SKILLS.how: Use the free tier and build one real deployment. Certifications matter far less than having hosted something.

SKILLS.label: CI/CD
SKILLS.what: Automating testing and deployment so that shipping stops being an event and starts being routine.
SKILLS.how: Put one project behind a pipeline that runs its tests and deploys on every push.

SKILLS.label: Testing
SKILLS.what: Proving your code does what you think before other people find out what it actually does.
SKILLS.how: Test the logic you were least sure about, not the logic that is obviously right.

SKILLS.label: DSA & problem solving
SKILLS.what: The single biggest filter in Indian technical interviews, and the reason a lot of good developers get rejected.
SKILLS.how: Solve a few problems every day for two months rather than cramming for a week before an interview.

SKILLS.label: Figma
SKILLS.what: The industry-standard tool for designing interfaces, used by both designers and developers.
SKILLS.how: Learn auto-layout and components, because those two save hours on every file after the first week.

SKILLS.label: UI/UX design
SKILLS.what: Deciding not just what something looks like but whether it can be used by a tired person on a bad connection.
SKILLS.how: Run three usability tests on people outside tech and actually change your design because of what they say.

SKILLS.label: Photoshop
SKILLS.what: Raster image editing, and still a hard requirement in print, e-commerce and marketing work.
SKILLS.how: Learn retouching and layer basics, then move to something that produces results rather than just effects.

SKILLS.label: Illustrator
SKILLS.what: Vector artwork, which is what logos, icons and print actually need because it scales without blurring.
SKILLS.how: Redesign three existing logos in vector and explain the grid logic behind each.

SKILLS.label: Video editing
SKILLS.what: Turning raw footage into something that holds attention, which is a genuine and portable creative skill.
SKILLS.how: Cut three finished pieces on real deadlines, one of them for someone who is not a friend.

SKILLS.label: SEO
SKILLS.what: Getting pages found in search results, and the technical half of it as much as the keyword half.
SKILLS.how: Take one site you own and fix its real crawl and speed problems before touching keywords at all.

SKILLS.label: Content writing
SKILLS.what: Writing that makes a reader do something, which is the hardest part of most marketing jobs.
SKILLS.how: Write fifty pieces and publish them. Volume teaches judgement that no course will.

SKILLS.label: Social media
SKILLS.what: Building an audience and a community, and reading what a platform is actually rewarding right now.
SKILLS.how: Grow one account to a few thousand real followers. It is a portfolio you cannot fake.

SKILLS.label: Paid advertising
SKILLS.what: Buying attention in a measurable way, which is the most direct bridge between marketing and money.
SKILLS.how: Run a small live campaign with a real budget and report the cost per result honestly.

SKILLS.label: Analytics
SKILLS.what: Measuring what actually happened, which is what separates marketing from guessing.
SKILLS.how: Set up tracking on a real site and explain one surprising number it revealed.

SKILLS.label: Excel
SKILLS.what: Still the most-used analytical tool in most Indian offices, well above what people expect.
SKILLS.how: Learn pivot tables, lookups and basic Power Query. That is the whole useful surface.

SKILLS.label: Power BI / Tableau
SKILLS.what: Turning data into dashboards people actually use to make decisions.
SKILLS.how: Build one dashboard from a public dataset and make it readable by someone who knows nothing about the data.

SKILLS.label: Machine learning
SKILLS.what: Systems that find patterns in data instead of following rules a person wrote out by hand.
SKILLS.how: Do the maths first. A framework used before you understand what it is optimising is guesswork.

SKILLS.label: PyTorch / TensorFlow
SKILLS.what: The main libraries for building and training neural networks, and what most applied AI job ads ask for.
SKILLS.how: Build a small model from scratch before you use a library to do it for you.

SKILLS.label: Statistics
SKILLS.what: Knowing whether a number means anything, which is the difference between analysis and noise.
SKILLS.how: Learn probability and hypothesis testing properly, not just the formula list for an exam.

SKILLS.label: pandas & NumPy
SKILLS.what: The core tools for handling tabular data in Python, and used in almost every data role.
SKILLS.how: Load a messy real dataset, clean it, and write down every decision you made along the way.

SKILLS.label: Communication
SKILLS.what: Explaining your work to people who do not have your context, which decides almost every promotion.
SKILLS.how: Do one short talk a month about something technical. It is the highest-leverage habit in this list.

SKILLS.label: Agile / Scrum
SKILLS.what: How modern teams plan, track and ship work in short cycles.
SKILLS.how: Run a sprint for a student project or club, with real standups and a real backlog.

SKILLS.label: Product thinking
SKILLS.what: Deciding what to build and why, which is the actual skill behind most senior roles.
SKILLS.how: Argue for one specific product change using evidence, then go build a rough version of it.

SKILLS.label: Networking
SKILLS.what: How machines actually reach each other, and the foundation of every security and infrastructure role.
SKILLS.how: Set up two machines on one network and trace every packet between them.

SKILLS.label: Security basics
SKILLS.what: Knowing how systems are actually broken into, which is the honest starting point for defending them.
SKILLS.how: Complete guided labs on deliberately vulnerable machines before touching a real system.

fullstack.label: Full-Stack Developer
fullstack.blurb: Builds both the interface people see and the logic behind it.
fullstack.what: You own a feature end to end: the page, the API, the database and the deployment. In small Indian teams this is usually the most common engineering role.
fullstack.how: Get one stack genuinely deep, ship four real projects, and be able to talk about every line in the codebase. Breadth matters less than one thing done properly.
phases: Learn HTML, CSS and JavaScript properly. Most people skip this and it shows forever. Do not touch a framework yet.
Pick one framework and one server language. Build a real app with a login and a database, not a tutorial clone.
Ship two more projects with tests, deployment and a README. Start applying before you feel ready, because you are nearly ready.
Specialise deliberately: deeper backend, more scale, or better performance. This is where a mid-level role starts paying properly.

frontend.label: Frontend Developer
frontend.blurb: Builds the part of the product people actually touch.
frontend.what: You turn designs into fast, accessible, responsive interfaces. Strong demand in India and the easiest engineering path to get into first.
frontend.how: Master the browser, not just the framework. Learn how the DOM, rendering and accessibility actually work, then apply that to real design files.
phases: Become genuinely good at HTML and CSS. Build layouts by hand before any framework helps you.
Learn JavaScript properly, including the DOM and async. This is the step that decides whether the job is available to you.
Learn one framework, then rebuild a real website from a Figma file. Pixel accuracy is the interview test.
Move into performance, accessibility and testing, which is what separates a mid-level from a junior frontend role.

backend.label: Backend Developer
backend.blurb: Builds the logic, data and reliability behind the product.
backend.what: You design APIs, model data, and make systems that stay correct under load. The most reliable hiring market in Indian software.
backend.how: One server language, real relational database modelling, and deployed services you have actually debugged at 2am.
phases: Pick one server language and learn its type system and error handling properly, not just syntax.
Learn SQL deeply and model a real domain. Data modelling is most of backend work and the least taught.
Build an API, document it, deploy it, and put a real front end in front of it so it has a user.
Add testing, caching and observability. Learn to read a flame graph and a slow query plan.

dataanalyst.label: Data Analyst
dataanalyst.blurb: Turns records into decisions people can act on.
dataanalyst.what: You answer business questions with data and present the answer clearly. The most transferable skill in the current job market.
dataanalyst.how: SQL to a professional level, one BI tool, and a portfolio of real analyses with written conclusions rather than pretty charts.
phases: SQL until joins and window functions are boring. It is the one skill that cannot be skipped in this role.
Learn statistics and statistics again, properly, and start using a BI tool on real datasets.
Build three full analyses on public data, each ending in a written recommendation. Presentation is half the job.
Add Python for automation and larger datasets, and learn to design the tracking that makes future analysis possible.

datascience.label: Data Scientist
datascience.blurb: Models data to answer questions statistics alone cannot.
datascience.what: You go beyond describing what happened to predicting and explaining why. Strong demand, but fewer openings than analyst roles.
datascience.how: Statistics and Python genuinely first, then modelling, and publish work with honest validation rather than a single impressive-looking number.
phases: Python for data and real statistics, including probability and hypothesis testing. Do not skip this to reach the fun part.
Classical modelling: regression, trees, validation and how to avoid fooling yourself with bad evaluation.
Work on real Kaggle problems end to end and write up the reasoning, including what did not work.
Specialise into deep learning or move toward ML engineering, and add SQL because production work lives in databases.

mlengineer.label: ML Engineer
mlengineer.blurb: Gets models into production where they can be trusted.
mlengineer.what: You build, train, deploy and monitor models in production. Closer to software engineering than to research, and currently well paid.
mlengineer.how: Software engineering skills plus real machine learning. The people who do well here can do both, not one or the other.
phases: Python properly, then linear algebra and probability at a working level, not just exam level.
Classical machine learning by hand. Understand gradient descent rather than calling a library function.
Build two end-to-end projects: data, model, evaluation, and an honest account of where it fails.
Productionise it: API, container, monitoring and retraining. Most ML jobs are won or lost on this step.

devops.label: DevOps Engineer
devops.blurb: Makes software reliable to ship and reliable to run.
devops.what: You own deployment, infrastructure, monitoring and reliability. Fewer openings than development, but a genuine shortage of skilled people.
devops.how: Linux deeply, then containers, then one cloud properly. Learn by breaking things deliberately and reading the logs.
phases: Get genuinely comfortable in Linux. No GUI escape hatches, and learn to read logs and processes properly.
Containers from first principles: build one, run one, break one. Understand what an image layer actually is.
One cloud platform properly, plus CI/CD on a real project with automated tests blocking deploys.
Orchestration, monitoring and cost. Learning to sleep at night because your systems page you is the real qualification.

cybersecurity.label: Cyber Security Analyst
cybersecurity.blurb: Finds the holes before somebody else does.
cybersecurity.what: You assess systems, detect attacks and close weaknesses. Growing fast in India, and every sector now has a compliance requirement.
cybersecurity.how: Practice on deliberately vulnerable systems. Theory-only study is the single most common reason candidates stall here.
phases: Networking and Linux properly, because everything else in security depends on understanding them.
Guided labs from the bottom up. Solve a few hundred deliberately vulnerable machines.
Pick a direction: web app security, network, or reverse engineering, and go deep in it rather than broad.
Get a recognised certification, then do real bug bounty work so you have findings you can show.

uiux.label: UI/UX Designer
uiux.blurb: Decides how a product looks, works and feels to the person using it.
uiux.what: You research users, design the interface, and test it until it works. Real demand, and one of the few non-engineering tech paths that pays well.
uiux.how: Four deep portfolio projects with reasoning shown, and real usability testing with people. A gallery of screens is not a portfolio.
phases: Learn Figma properly, including auto-layout and components, then redesign one app you use daily.
Study usability and layout principles, and start writing why you made each decision.
Run real usability tests and redesign based on what breaks. This is the step most portfolios skip.
Specialise towards product design, and learn enough HTML and CSS to be taken seriously by engineers.

marketing.label: Digital Marketer
marketing.blurb: Drives demand and growth using content, search, social and ads.
marketing.what: You get people to find a product and then do something about it. The broadest set of entry-level routes into tech-adjacent work.
marketing.how: Own one channel end to end, with real numbers. Campaigns you can point at beat certificates every time.
phases: Understand one channel properly, whether it is search, social or ads, including how the platform ranks or charges.
Write and publish consistently. Content is the part most people avoid and the part that compounds.
Run a live campaign with real money and report cost per result honestly, including what failed.
Add analytics and build a repeatable process, which is what turns a marketer into someone a company will pay senior rates.

productmanager.label: Product Manager
productmanager.blurb: Decides what gets built, in what order, and why.
productmanager.what: You sit between users, design and engineering and own the outcome of a product area. High ceiling, and the hardest role to self-teach into.
productmanager.how: Analyse a product you use, write the argument for a change with evidence, and get it in front of working engineers.
phases: Learn to read data well enough to be useful in a roadmap argument. SQL is the practical tool here.
Study how products are decided, and write analyses of real product choices with your own alternatives argued fairly.
Get into an internship, ideally in a small team where you can own a feature end to end.
Build a track record of decisions that shipped and worked. This role is bought on judgement, and judgement is only proven by outcomes.

mobile.label: Mobile App Developer
mobile.blurb: Builds the software people carry with them all day.
mobile.what: You develop apps for Android, iOS or both. Fewer dedicated openings than web, but a distinct and stable skill.
mobile.how: One platform first, React Native or Flutter, and ship a real app to a store. The deployment step teaches the most.
phases: Get the language genuinely solid first. Cross-platform frameworks hide the fundamentals and it shows later.
Learn one framework and build an app that does something real with device permissions and local storage.
Ship it to a store, handle real installs and crashes, and fix what breaks on real devices.
Add backend services, offline support and performance work, which is where mobile roles get more senior.

GENERIC_ITEM.what: This is something you typed in yourself, so there is no fixed description attached to it. What it turns into depends almost entirely on how concretely you apply it.
GENERIC_ITEM.how: Turn it into something a stranger can look at within a month — a project, a post, a competition entry, a session you ran. Anything you can point to beats anything you can describe.

GENERIC_PHASES: Pick one concrete thing you want to be able to do in three months, and write down what already stands between you and it. That gap is your first plan.
Learn the smallest useful slice of that, and build something small and finished. Finishing early matters more than finishing perfectly.
Show it to people who will be blunt about it, then fix what they hit. Exposure to real reactions is the part nobody can shortcut.
Specialise, keep a visible record of what you can do, and start applying well before you feel ready. Readiness is decided by the work, not the feeling.
